before.quote:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. The boundary patches have continuous outward Euclidean unit normal $n$. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$ measured in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$ measured in $\mathrm{Pa}$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$

All derivatives below are Cartesian derivatives in this fixed chart; the positive coordinate rescaling defined below is not a change of observer.

For a scalar field $f$, $\nabla_x f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$.

Define the dimensionless coordinates and their domains by
$$\Theta=\frac{Ut}{L},\qquad X=\frac{x}{L},\qquad I^*=\left\{\frac{Ut}{L}:t\in I\right\},\qquad \Omega^*=\left\{\frac{x}{L}:x\in\Omega\right\}.$$

In the first, force-free branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time partial derivatives and continuous first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let the pressure field $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with continuous first spatial partial derivatives. $$\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}_x\sigma,\qquad (\operatorname{div}_x\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij},$$

The coefficient identities do not assert an incompressible or inviscid limit, an error bound, uniqueness, identical solutions for different geometries or rescaled data, or a turbulence threshold. They are conditional predictions of the adopted model formulations and are not experimental observations or proof that either model describes a material.

before.quote:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. $$\rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=0.$$
Here $p$ is a constraint multiplier. No viscous stress or equation of state is included. Initial, wall, periodic and other boundary data are separate inputs. This is an adopted model formulation, not a derivation of empirical validity or an assertion of solution existence.

Let $D=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0\}$, let $\rho_0>0$, $p_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\kappa\ne0$. On $D$ define

$$u_v(x,y,z)=\left(-\frac{\kappa y}{r^2},\frac{\kappa x}{r^2},0\right),\qquad p_v(x,y,z)=p_0-\frac{\rho_0\kappa^2}{2r^2}.$$

For every $R>0$ and fixed $z_0$, the positively oriented circle $\gamma_R(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,R\sin\theta,z_0)$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, has circulation $\oint_{\gamma_R}u_v\cdot d\mathbf r=2\pi\kappa$. Consequently no single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi:D\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $u_v=\nabla\phi$ on all of $D$, even though $\operatorname{curl}u_v=0$ there. $$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

This smooth steady field is divergence-free and satisfies the same constant-density equation for every $\nu>0$. For this steady field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $\gamma:J\to\mathbb R^3$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $\gamma'(s)=u_s(\gamma(s))$. Its Bernoulli quantity $B=|u_s|^2/2+p_s/\rho_0=p_0/\rho_0+\Omega_0^2r^2$ is constant along each streamline and takes different values at distinct radii. $$\partial_tu_v+(u_v\cdot\nabla)u_v+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p_v-\nu\Delta u_v=0$$

holds for every $\nu>0$, with $\partial_tu_v=0$.

Separately, for $\Omega_0\ne0$ set $u_s=(-\Omega_0y,\Omega_0x,0)$ and $p_s=p_0+\rho_0\Omega_0^2r^2/2$ on $\mathbb R^3$. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. $$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$

Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. abla p+\mu\Delta u+ho_0b=0$. The Postulate does not assert that small Reynolds number alone yields this branch, provide an approximation error or solution-existence result, or establish empirical validity. Boundary and far-field data remain separate.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

Here $F$ and $J$ are dimensionless and $A$ has units metres. The material map $\chi$ describes motion of the medium; it is not a change of observer or frame. The Eulerian velocity is the vector field defined by $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$, measured in m s$^{-1}$. For a differentiable scalar or component field $f$, its material derivative is $D_tf=\partial_tf+u\cdot\nabla f$. Set $L_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, $W=(L-L^T)/2$, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D=\operatorname{div}u$, and $D_0=D-(\theta/3)I_3$; $L,D,W,\theta,D_0$ have units s$^{-1}$. Define vorticity by

$$\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\ \partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\ \partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x),$$

also in s$^{-1}$. In this library, a motion is **material-incompressible** on a region when $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there; **spatially homogeneous density** means $\nabla\rho=0$ there. A **streamline at time $t_0$** is a $C^1$ integral curve satisfying $dX/ds=u(t_0,X(s))$ for a frozen $t_0$, with curve parameter $s$ measured in seconds. These are different constructions for an unsteady field.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. before.quote: > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection $\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]], [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters $x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give $m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so $m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure $m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures, and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them on the entire Borel sigma-algebra ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on $\mathbb T^n$ ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation (by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$. Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion, nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters proved below.

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$; 2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$; 3. consequently the Fourier expansion $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$ hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and 4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

after.quote: Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $u,v\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $f$ and $g$ be integrable between $u$ and $v$.
If $\eta\ge0$ and

$$|f(x)-g(x)|\le\eta$$

throughout the closed interval with endpoints $u$ and $v$, then

$$\left|\int_u^v f-\int_u^v g\right|\le \eta\,|v-u|.$$

Its derivative is $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$.

For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. Then $\int H=0$ by [A2]. Assuming the construction in dimension $d-1$, define
$$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$
Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes both before the support and after its total first-coordinate integral, which is zero; the other components are compactly supported by induction.

If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the support of $\theta_i$; for the first component also include the interval hull of these supports. The recursive formulas then place every output component inside the fixed compact product $K'=\prod_iJ_i$. Every output derivative is a finite sum of fixed-bump derivatives times finite-coordinate integrals of derivatives of $h$ or its marginals. Such integrals have sup norm at most the interval length times the integrand sup norm, and differentiation in other coordinates commutes with integration. Induction therefore bounds each output seminorm by a constant times finitely many input seminorms. This proves fixed-support continuity.

after.claim:
For the given rectangle, fix once for all inputs and support sets an affine copy of the bump in
[A1] on each side interval. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of
rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than
every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. By [F1] its continuous compact-interval integral exists; positivity makes it nonzero, so
normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. The primitive
difference quotient differs from $h(x)$ by at most $\sup\{|h(s)-h(x)|:s\text{ lies between }x\text{
and }x+\delta\}$, which tends to zero by continuity. Its derivative is therefore $h$, and it
vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its
support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the
zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$.

Here and below the coordinate integrals of smooth compactly supported functions may be computed
on the closed coordinate intervals after extension by zero. This extension is smooth on a
neighborhood of the closed box: compact support leaves a neighborhood of every boundary face where
the function is zero. By [F1] the function and every coordinate section are Riemann integrable;
[F2], applied to successive coordinate blocks, identifies all iterated orders with the same box
integral. In particular, the marginal $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$ has total integral equal
to $\int_\Omega h$.

To differentiate a marginal, fix all other coordinates and restrict the differentiated
coordinate to a compact interval inside its open side interval. The integrand and each parameter
derivative are continuous on the resulting compact two-variable rectangle, so repeated [F3] gives
$$\partial_{x'}^\beta H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}\partial_{x'}^\beta h(s,x')\,ds,\qquad \sup|\partial^\beta H|\le (b_1-a_1)\sup|\partial_{x'}^\beta h|.$$
The inequality follows from [F4] with the second integrand zero. Continuity of these derivatives
jointly in the remaining parameters follows from the same bound applied to their differences and
uniform continuity of the integrand derivative on each compact box.

The same reasoning differentiates an integral with upper endpoint $x_1$ in its other parameters.
For its $x_1$ derivative, the difference quotient of $\int_{a_1}^{x_1}f(s,x')\,ds$ differs from
$f(x_1,x')$ by at most $\sup_{s\text{ between }x_1\text{ and }x_1+\delta}|f(s,x')-f(x_1,x')|$, which
tends to zero by continuity; higher endpoint derivatives then follow by ordinary differentiation.
This proves the finite-integral identities used in the recursion.

For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. By step 1.2, $\int
H=\int h=0$, and steps 1.3–2.1 show that $H$ and the displayed primitives are smooth. Assuming the
construction in dimension $d-1$, define
$$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$
Differentiating gives $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h-\theta_1H+\theta_1H=h$. The first component vanishes
both before the support and after its total first-coordinate integral, which is zero; the other
components are compactly supported by induction.

If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly
contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the
support of the already fixed bump $\theta_i$. Their product is a common compact output-support set
$K'=\prod_iJ_i$: before the first-coordinate support the primitive is zero, and after it the
primitive is zero because its full first-coordinate integral is zero; the other components have the
required support by induction.

Write $p_m(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup|\partial^\alpha f|$, taking the maximum also over
components for vector fields, and put $\ell_1=b_1-a_1$. Step 1.3 gives $p_m(H)\le\ell_1p_m(h)$. For
the first component in step 3.1, a derivative with no $x_1$ differentiation is an integral of
$\partial_{x'}^\beta h-\theta_1\partial_{x'}^\beta H$ and is bounded by
$\ell_1(1+\ell_1\|\theta_1\|_\infty)p_m(h)$. If the derivative differentiates $x_1$ at least once,
the endpoint identity in step 2.1 gives a derivative of $h$ minus a fixed derivative of $\theta_1$
times a derivative of $H$, again bounded by a constant times $p_m(h)$. For each remaining component
$\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')$, the product derivative is bounded by a fixed bump-derivative
constant times $p_m(R'H)\le C'_m p_m(H)$ by induction. The dimension-one bounds in step 1.1 start
this induction. Thus
$$p_m(Rh)\le C_m p_m(h)\qquad(m\ge0),$$
where $C_m$ depends only on the fixed rectangle, bumps, dimension and $m$, not on $h$. These are all
fixed-support seminorm estimates, proving the full stated continuity. Every displayed construction
is linear in $h$, and the bumps were fixed once independently of $h$ and $K$, so the same map $R$
serves all compact input supports.

before.quote: For an integer $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$, and the characters are $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$. For $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, set $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, componentwise, so real fields have $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. The completion is identified with its weighted coefficient space using finite symmetric cutoffs. If $s\ge0$, it has a unique $L^2$ representative; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice and fix $d\in\{1,2,3\}$. For a vector Fourier coefficient $a(k)\in\mathbb C^d$, define $(Pa)(k)=P_ka(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, where $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k
e0$. For a tensor field $F=(F_{ij})_{i,j=1}^d$ with coefficients in any $H^s(Q_d)$, define the scalar pressure map $Q$ by $\widehat{QF}(0)=0$ and $\widehat{QF}(k)=-\sum_{i,j=1}^d k_i k_j|k|^{-2}\widehat F_{ij}(k)$ for $k
e0$. For $q\in H^s(Q_d)$, define $\partial_jq\in H^{s-1}(Q_d)$ coefficientwise by $\widehat{\partial_jq}(k)=ik_j\widehat q(k)$; for vector fields set $\widehat{
abla q}(k)=ik\widehat q(k)$, and for tensor fields set $\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}_i(k)=i\sum_jk_j\widehat F_{ij}(k)$. These derivative maps are bounded from $H^s$ to $H^{s-1}$. The multipliers $P$ and $Q$ are real-preserving and bounded on every $H^s$, $s\in\mathbb R$; $P$ is an orthogonal projection and commutes with these derivatives. For every $F$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, their exact identity is the coefficientwise equality
$$\widehat{
abla QF}(k)=-(I-P_k)\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k).$$
In particular, both sides have zero coefficient at $k=0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and use $H^\sigma(Q_d)$ with the normalized measure and weights in the Definition. For every integer $j\ge0$ and $\sigma>j+d/2$, each scalar $q\in H^\sigma(Q_d)$ has a $C^j$ representative and $\|q\|_{C^j}\le C_{d,\sigma,j}\|q\|_{H^\sigma}$. For every $\sigma>d/2$, pointwise multiplication extends uniquely from trigonometric polynomials to a continuous bilinear map $H^\sigma\times H^\sigma\to H^\sigma$ satisfying $\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\le C_{d,\sigma}\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma}$. The assertions extend componentwise to finite-dimensional vector and tensor fields.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $m\ge s\ge4$ be integers, let $f,g\in C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$, and define $\Lambda^m$ by $\widehat{\Lambda^m q}(k)=w_k^m\widehat q(k)$. For each coordinate $j$,
$$\|[\Lambda^m,f]\partial_jg\|_{L^2}\le C_{d,m,s}\bigl(\|f\|_{H^m}\|g\|_{H^s}+\|f\|_{H^s}\|g\|_{H^m}\bigr),$$
where $[\Lambda^m,f]h=\Lambda^m(fh)-f\Lambda^mh$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $N\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be a polynomial map, and let $T_*>0$. If $x\in C^1([0,T_*),\mathbb R^N)$ solves $x'(t)=F(x(t))$ and there is $R\ge0$ such that $\|x(t)\|_2\le R$ for every $0\le t<T_*$, then there are $\epsilon>0$ and a solution $\widetilde x\in C^1([0,T_*+\epsilon),\mathbb R^N)$ of the same ODE with $\widetilde x(t)=x(t)$ for $0\le t<T_*$. Thus a finite right endpoint of a bounded finite-dimensional polynomial ODE trajectory is extendible.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ have normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_j\alpha_j$ and $\partial^\alpha=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_d^{\alpha_d}$. Give $C^\infty(Q_d;\mathbb R)$ the Fr'echet topology generated by $p_m(\phi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\phi\|_\infty$, for $m\in\mathbb N_0$, where the derivatives are those of the smooth periodic lift to $\mathbb R^d$. A periodic distribution is a continuous real-linear functional on this test space, extended complex-linearly to complex-valued tests. For such a distribution $S$, define $\widehat S(k)=\langle S,e^{-ik\cdot x}angle$ for $e_k(x)=e^{ik\cdot x}$ and define its mean to be $\widehat S(0)=\langle S,1angle$. For an integrable function $g$, the pairing is $\langle g,\phiangle=\int_{Q_d}g\phi\,d\mu$. Define distributional derivatives by $\langle\partial_jS,\phiangle=-\langle S,\partial_j\phiangle$. For a smooth scalar test, $
abla\phi=(\partial_1\phi,\ldots,\partial_d\phi)$ and $\Delta\phi=\sum_j\partial_j^2\phi$; for a smooth vector field $v$, $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_j\partial_jv_j$, $(v\otimes v)_{ij}=v_iv_j$, and $(v\cdot
abla)v_i=\sum_jv_j\partial_jv_i$. In particular, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ distributionally means $-\int_{Q_d}u\cdot
abla\phi\,d\mu=0$ for every real test function $\phi$. Equality of periodic distributions means equality on every such test function. Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $s>d/2+1$, and let $u\in H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in this sense. Then $u\otimes u\in H^s$, the mean-zero scalar $\pi=Q(u\otimes u)$ belongs to $H^s$, and in $H^{s-1}$,
$$P(u\cdot
abla u)=u\cdot
abla u+
abla\pi.$$
Among mean-zero periodic distributions $\widetilde\pi$ for which this identity holds as an equality of periodic distributions, this pressure is unique. The formula is a torus pressure recovery result and asserts no wall pressure regularity.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, $T>0$, and $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized measure $d\mu=(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For $z:Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, use componentwise Fourier coefficients $\widehat z(k)=\int_{Q_d}z(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$, weights $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$, and the weighted coefficient completion norm $\|z\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat z(k)|^2$; the normalized Fourier isometry gives $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat z(k)|^2$, where $\|z\|_2=(\int_{Q_d}|z|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$ and the pointwise component norm is Euclidean. In particular, $H^0=L^2$. For a map $z:[0,T]\times Q_d\to\mathbb R^M$, smooth on the closed cylinder means that for every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and spatial multi-index $\alpha$, $\partial_t^m\partial_x^\alpha z$ exists on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and extends continuously to $[0,T]\times Q_d$; spatial derivatives are those of its periodic lift. For a spatial vector field define $\operatorname{div}z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jz_j$ and $\Delta z=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_j^2z$. Write $\nabla z$ for the spatial Jacobian and $\|\nabla z(t)\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in Q_d}|\nabla z(t,x)|_F$, where $|\cdot|_F$ is the Euclidean Frobenius matrix norm. Let $P$ be the coefficientwise vector multiplier with $P_0=I$ and $P_k=I-kk^{\mathsf T}/|k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. The equations below hold pointwise on $(0,T)\times Q_d$ and at the time endpoints by continuous extension.

(i) If $\nu\ge0$ and $u,v\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{u,v\}$,
$$z_t+P((z\cdot\nabla)z)=\nu\Delta z,\qquad \operatorname{div}z=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$, with $w=u-v$,
$$\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(2\int_0^t\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_\infty\,d\tau\right).$$

(ii) Let $N\ge1$ and, for $1\le j\le d$, let $A_j:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ be a fixed real-linear map whose image consists of symmetric matrices. If $q,r\in C^\infty([0,T]\times Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy, for each $z\in\{q,r\}$,
$$z_t+\sum_{j=1}^dA_j(z)\partial_jz=0,$$
then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|q(t)-r(t)\|_2^2\le\|q(0)-r(0)\|_2^2\exp\!\left(C_{d,N,A}\int_0^t(\|\nabla q(\tau)\|_\infty+\|\nabla r(\tau)\|_\infty)\,d\tau\right),$$
where $C_{d,N,A}$ depends only on $d,N$ and the operator norms of the finitely many maps $A_j$. For either pair $(z_1,z_2)=(u,v)$ or $(q,r)$, put $w=z_1-z_2$. Let $\Gamma\ge0$ be any uniform rate for which the corresponding squared $L^2$ estimate above gives $\|w(t)\|_2^2\le\|w(0)\|_2^2e^{\Gamma t}$. If $s\ge1$ and $\max_{t\in[0,T]}\max(\|z_1(t)\|_{H^s},\|z_2(t)\|_{H^s})\le M$ for some $M\ge0$, define
$$B_s(M)=\begin{cases}1,&s=1,\\(2M)^{(s-1)/s},&s>1.\end{cases}$$
Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|w(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le B_s(M)\|w(0)\|_2^{1/s}e^{\Gamma t/(2s)}.$$
These are conditional estimates for already given smooth maps on the stated cylinder and assert no existence theorem. All quantities are mathematical and no physical units are assigned to $\nu$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** is an event-coordinate map $(t,X)\mapsto(t,x_t(X))$, where $b:E\to\mathbb R^3$ is an orientation-preserving affine isometry, $w\in\mathbb R^3$ is constant, and $x_t(X)=b(X)+tw$ for $t\in I$. The affine map $b$ is auxiliary data defined on $E$, so this formula requires no evaluation at time $0$ when $0\notin I$. Each fixed-time spatial map is an orientation-preserving affine isometry with fixed spatial orientation; the spatial origin has constant velocity. Spatial coordinates are measured in metres and $w$ in metres per second. A chart may also use a translated absolute-time coordinate; at corresponding events the inertial-chart transformations are the ones displayed below. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

Use the Newtonian spacetime and Cartesian inertial-chart convention from the earlier definition titled “Classical frames, primitive quantities and SI units”: time is absolute, $M$ is an oriented Euclidean affine three-space with no distinguished origin, and a Cartesian inertial chart is an orientation-preserving affine isometry $X:M\to\mathbb R^3$ paired with that time coordinate. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Let $c_v>0$ be the adopted specific-heat-at-constant-volume parameter and $R>0$ the adopted specific gas-constant parameter, each in joules per kilogram kelvin. Define the derived specific heat at constant pressure and ratio of specific heats by $c_p:=c_v+R$ and $\gamma:=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$. Choose $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\in\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin as reference data. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation
$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define the thermodynamic temperature and pressure maps by $T(v,s):=\partial_s e(v,s)$ and $p(v,s):=-\partial_v e(v,s)$, holding the other state coordinate fixed. Direct differentiation gives
$$T(v,s)=\frac{e(v,s)}{c_v}>0,\qquad p(v,s)=(\gamma-1)\frac{e(v,s)}{v}>0.$$
For density and entropy coordinates define the state-pressure map $p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=p(1/\rho,s)$ for $\rho>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. The spacetime state map is $v(t,x):=1/\rho(t,x)$ and $(t,x)\mapsto(v(t,x),s(t,x))\in\mathcal U$. It assigns the specific internal-energy, temperature, and thermodynamic-pressure fields by
$$e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad T(t,x):=(\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$
Consequently $T(t,x)=e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/c_v$ and $p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)=(\gamma-1)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/v(t,x)=(\gamma-1)\rho(t,x)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)=R\rho(t,x)T(t,x)$. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m(t,x):=\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\rho(t,x)(e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. $$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\right),\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}}.$$

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,
